items.title: Artificial Intelligence Use and Learner Autonomy Among Secondary Students: The Roles of AI Literacy and Metacognitive Self-Regulation
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary education has created new opportunities for personalized support, immediate feedback, problem-solving, and self-directed learning, while also raising concerns about students’ reliance on AI-generated information. This narrative literature review examined AI use and learner autonomy among secondary students, with particular attention to the roles of AI literacy and metacognitive self-regulation. Recent literature published primarily from 2021 to 2026 was identified, screened, and synthesized through narrative and reflexive thematic analysis. Across the reviewed studies, AI supported learner autonomy most clearly when students used it for exploration, feedback, problem-solving, and self-regulated learning rather than as a substitute for independent thinking. AI literacy helped students understand AI, evaluate generated information, recognize its limitations, and make responsible decisions about its use. Metacognitive self-regulation, in turn, supported students in planning, monitoring, and evaluating their learning while working with AI. The literature also pointed to challenges, including excessive reliance on AI, limited AI knowledge, inconsistent learner engagement, and differences in self-regulatory abilities. Overall, learner autonomy in AI-supported settings depends on how students use the technology and on the development of AI literacy and metacognitive self-regulation with appropriate teacher guidance. The study contributes primarily to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by supporting responsible and learner-centered integration of AI in secondary education. From a sustainability perspective, strengthening students’ critical and self-regulatory competencies may promote more responsible, adaptable, and sustainable use of emerging digital technologies in education.

items.title: Artificial intelligence use, creative thinking disposition, and metacognitive awareness among EFL learners: a structural equation modelling approach
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in English as a foreign language (EFL) learning, yet its cognitive implications depend on how learners engage with it rather than on its use alone. This study examined the structural relationships among differentiated patterns of AI use, creative thinking disposition, and metacognitive awareness among undergraduate EFL learners. Using a quantitative cross-sectional correlational design, data were collected from 713 learners and analysed through structural equation modelling. AI use was conceptualised as cognitive-support use, creative-extension use, reproductive or substitutive use, and ethical and critical awareness. The findings indicate that the use of cognitive-support and creative-extension AI is positively associated with both creative thinking disposition and metacognitive awareness. In contrast, reproductive or substitutive use is negatively associated with these outcomes. Creative thinking disposition demonstrates a strong positive relationship with metacognitive awareness and mediates the effects of constructive AI use on regulatory awareness. Ethical and critical engagement with AI moderates these relationships, strengthening the positive associations between constructive AI use and both creative and metacognitive outcomes. The results clarify that the cognitive value of AI in EFL learning is shaped by learner agency, reflective judgement, and responsibility for meaning-making. The study advances a cognitively grounded account of AI-mediated EFL learning and provides empirical support for differentiating AI engagement patterns in both research and instructional design.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Theranostics: Integrating Machine Learning For Precision Diagnosis And Personalized Therapy
items.abstract: Theranostics links disease characterization with treatment selection and response assessment, creating a framework in which diagnostic information directly informs individualized therapy. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), deep learning, radiomics, radiogenomics, and multimodal data integration are expanding this concept from target verification toward quantitative prediction of diagnosis, prognosis, therapeutic response, dose, and toxicity. This review examines how AI can connect imaging, electronic health records, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, pharmacogenomics, and treatment response data across a unified theranostic workflow. Evidence from ophthalmology, dermatology, pathology, cardiology, oncology, drug response prediction, radiopharmaceutical therapy, and personalized dosing demonstrates that ML models can extract clinically useful patterns from complex datasets and support patient level stratification. In nuclear medicine, AI assisted segmentation, quantitative imaging, and dosimetry may shorten analysis time and facilitate patient-specific radiopharmaceutical therapy. In precision oncology, radiomics and radiogenomics can associate imaging phenotypes with molecular characteristics and treatment outcomes, while computational drug response models can prioritize therapies for molecularly defined disease. However, clinical translation remains constrained by dataset shift, limited external validation, data leakage, class imbalance, algorithmic bias, interpretability, privacy, interoperability, regulatory uncertainty, and insufficient prospective evidence. Future progress will require multicenter datasets, standardized data pipelines, transparent reporting, calibrated uncertainty, explainable models, federated or privacy preserving learning, prospective clinical trials, and continuous post deployment monitoring. AI driven theranostics is therefore best viewed as a decision support ecosystem in which computational prediction complements, rather than replaces, clinical expertise and experimentally validated treatment pathways.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-enabled value creation and competitive advantage in marketing: A dynamic capabilities perspective
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities contribute to marketing value creation and competitive advantage by integrating customer data, marketing intelligence, operational execution, and human strategic oversight. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combined a survey of 300 marketing executives with qualitative evidence from three digital-first brand cases to examine AI maturity, predictive analytics, marketing integration, automation, and performance outcomes. Organizations with higher AI maturity reported 25.4% lower customer acquisition costs (CAC) than those with lower AI maturity, while Generative AI (GenAI) users reported a 40% reduction in content-production time. Qualitative evidence indicates that predictive customer intelligence can enable more anticipatory and personalized engagement, while human oversight, data governance, and authenticity remain important boundary conditions. Synthetic data offers a complementary option for privacy-conscious experimentation and model development. The AI-Marketing Value Creation Model conceptualizes competitive advantage as the coordinated conversion of customer data and AI capabilities into economic, operational, and experiential value through organizational processes and human judgment. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Marketing Intelligence, Marketing Operations, Competitive Advantage, Dynamic Capabilities.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-enabled value creation and competitive advantage in supply chain management: A dynamic capabilities perspective
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) creates strategic value in supply chain management (SCM) by integrating technological capabilities, organizational agility, and human expertise. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines quantitative survey data from 250 global supply chain executives with three qualitative industry case studies to develop the Artificial Intelligence–Supply Chain Management (AI-SCM) Value Creation Framework, grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Organizations with higher AI maturity reported 31.5% higher demand-forecast accuracy and 14.5% lower logistics and freight costs. Qualitative evidence indicates that AI-enabled predictive analytics, adaptive decision-making, and operational integration can strengthen supply chain agility and resilience. AI can function as an embedded strategic capability when supported by organizational readiness, reliable data, and human expertise. However, these benefits are not unconditional. Environmental burdens associated with AI infrastructure and algorithmic management risks, including surveillance and reduced worker autonomy, require responsible governance and meaningful human oversight. AI-enabled value creation is therefore contingent on technological capability, organizational conditions, and responsible human-AI integration. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Supply Chain Management, Competitive Advantage, Dynamic Capabilities, Value Creation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence; Rethinking- Learning in an Era of HumanMade Technology and Capitalist Mechanism
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) have revolutionised the interaction between humans, knowledge and technology. What once needed years of formal education, years of institutional access or specialist's help is now obtained, translated, explained, reorganised in seconds. This unprecedented accessibility can help to minimize some of the age disadvantages in learning and provide lifelong education. Meanwhile, it asks the essential question: With the ready availability of answers, and analyses the decisions through own judgement, curiosity, critical understanding and intellectual independence. This paper critically discusses the overlaps between AI, Age, Education, Automation and Capitalism. But it's not necessarily the democratisation of education, it says, arguing that the democratisation of access to AI shouldn't be equated with the democratisation of education. While it can overturn the notion that technological skills are predominantly the purview of younger people, the potential for age disparities leading compounded differences in access to these tools, algorithmic bias, and confidence gaps and differences in digital and AI literacy. At the same time, the increasing machine-like nature of the educational activities threatening to change the purpose of education from learning and human development to efficiency, productivity and measurable outcome is awaited niche. Literature-based analysis is carried out by reference to the UNESCO, OECD, Stanford AI Index, IMF, ILO, and peer-reviewed scholarship along with the theoretical approaches of critical pedagogy, digital ageism and technological capitalism. Based on secondary data, the use of AI by students is already prevalent and evidence about the impacts on learning is mixed, and largely dependent on the context of use. This paper suggests neither technological rejection nor unconditional adoption. Rather, a human-centred approach should be pursued where AI is a tool for intellectual work and not an intellectual replacement in education systems. AI literacy, critical thinking, intergenerational learning, teacher agency, and transparent assessment and equitable access, therefore, should be central to modern education.

items.title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can contribute to the reasoning and communication represented in student work, complicating inferences from product quality to individual capability. This conceptual article develops an integrated framework for assessing cognitive ownership through mutual evaluation and outcome-aligned verification. Cognitive ownership is defined as a learner’s demonstrated capacity to understand, evaluate, adapt, and accept responsibility for consequential reasoning under specified conditions of assistance. Eight indicators are organized into four assessment domains: understanding, epistemic judgment, adaptive performance, and reflective accountability. Mutual evaluation combines independent student and instructor judgments, evidence-based comparison, and documented responses to disagreement; agreement is not treated as proof of learning. The framework distinguishes the quality of an AI-assisted product, capability demonstrated during assessment, and learning established through change and retention. A worked higher education example illustrates task design, scoring, and responses to conflicting evidence. Five propositions and a validation agenda address incremental predictive value, task sampling, feedback, fairness, and feasibility. The framework is proposed rather than empirically validated. Its contribution is to connect existing validity and evaluative judgment scholarship with a practical account of the evidence needed to support bounded claims about individual and assisted performance.

Re-entry authority is conferred only at a linearizable commit that consumes the reservation and nonce; eligibility, reservation and approval states confer none. Given a suitable resolver, liabilities and failure history charged to semantic families survive aliases, merges, splits, epoch changes and rollback; restoration reapplies current ledgers, not historical authority. Under stated premises, Proposition G6 keeps confirmed, unresolved and reserved liabilities and actual consumption within every attributed cap, and Proposition G4 excludes, until revalidation, dependent authorizations after trusted recognition of a required invalidation and dependent effects after a durable receiver fence. Propositions G7 and G8 order leases, bound delegation chains but not aggregates, and bound hysteretic switching by score variation. An output contract fixes what each state and record licenses. Explicit-state studies close finite configurations, yield counterexamples for deliberate guard and ledger mutations, and retain overdue-duty and partial-effect states. In their timing models, local receiver checks cannot exclude stale effects before the fence without refusing valid work; atomic checks of the input's state (not the trusted log) and pre-fenced controlled changes exclude them by construction. items.title: Automated Performance Evaluation and Due Process in Disciplinary Procedures
items.abstract: Digital technologies that are now increasingly being adopted in HRM have changed the way in which performance of employees is measured, monitored, evaluated, and managed. The systems for Automated Performance Evaluation (APE) make use of such technologies as rule-based scoring, key performance indicators (KPIs), machine learning, employee monitoring software, natural language processing (NLP), and Human Resource Information Systems (HRIS) for evaluating the behavior and performance of employees. While there is an array of advantages that the implementation of these technologies may bring, there are significant issues associated with the use of these technologies for disciplining. The score that is assigned by algorithms may have a bearing on any warning issued to the employee, development of performance improvement plan, suspension, promotion, termination, or any other decision affecting the employment. The study seeks to explore the link between automated performance evaluation and due process in workplace discipline proceedings. Concepts such as APE, algorithmic management, natural justice, and organizational justice will be developed. The study shall also explore technologies used in automatic evaluation of employee performances and how such technologies could be used in various phases of discipline processes. Special consideration shall be given to the right to notice, being given a chance to hear oneself, access to information/evidence, impartiality of decisions, explanations of algorithmic decisions, and the possibility of human review. Legal considerations include Indian labour laws and employment law principles, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 as well as the international approaches such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), EU Artificial Intelligence Act among others. The paper discusses some of the challenges associated with automated evaluation of employee performance such as opacity of algorithms, discrimination or bias, inaccuracies in the use of data, failure to take context into consideration, over monitoring, accountability issues, and power asymmetry. Finally, an automated evaluation process that is consistent with due process is developed.

items.title: Beyond AI Use: Examining The Predictive Quality of AI Dependency & Distress Intolerance in Avoidance Coping Among Young Adults in Mumbai
items.abstract: Abstract Background: As the reliance on AI keeps growing, it becomes important to understand its psychological implications. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI and mental health by investigating the predictive quality of AI dependency and distress tolerance in the use of avoidance coping in response to stressful situations. Aims: The present research aims to examine the predictive relationship between AI dependency, distress intolerance and avoidance coping among young adults in Mumbai. Method: 90 participants from Mumbai (60 Females, 29 Males) who were aged between 18-25 years (M=20.8, SD=2.38) and used AI apps like ChatGPT and Gemini, were selected using convenience sampling. All participants completed the Generative AI Dependency Scale (Goh et al., 2025), Distress Tolerance Scale (Simons & Gaher, 2005) and Ways of Coping Scale-Revised (Folkman & Lazarus, 1985). Correlation and simple linear regression was computed for statistical analysis. Results: Findings of the research indicate that AI dependency showed a significant positive correlation with avoidance coping (p < .01) and hence was a statistically significant predictor. Furthermore, distress intolerance showed a weak correlation with avoidance coping and was therefore not a statistically significant predictor (p > .05) of avoidance coping. Conclusion: The findings of this study highlight the predictive role of AI dependency in the use of avoidance coping when faced with stressful situations. The role of distress tolerance in avoidance coping needs to be studied further in a more diverse and larger population. The findings may help develop strategies that promote healthy coping skills in stressful situations in the era of increasing AI use.

items.title: Beyond the Black Box: Algorithmic Accountability and the Legal Regulation of Predictive Analytics and Machine Learning in India
items.abstract: The proliferation of predictive analytics and machine-learning systems has transformed decision-making across banking, insurance, healthcare, employment, policing, welfare administration, education and advertising in India. Algorithms no longer merely inform human choices; with increasing frequency they determine outcomes that affect individuals’ rights, livelihoods and opportunities. This transformation has produced what is commonly described as the “black box” problem: decisions are generated through processes that are technically complex, commercially proprietary and cognitively opaque, leaving affected persons unable to understand, contest or seek redress against them. Algorithmic systems trained on historical data further risk reproducing and amplifying existing patterns of discrimination against already disadvantaged groups. India’s existing legal architecture, anchored principally in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, offers meaningful safeguards for the processing of personal data but does not comprehensively regulate the algorithmic decisions that such data ultimately produces. Constitutional guarantees of equality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14 and of privacy, dignity and personal liberty under Article 21 supply an important normative foundation for extending accountability beyond data governance. This paper undertakes a doctrinal examination of algorithmic accountability in India through the interconnected lenses of privacy, equality, transparency, explainability, human oversight and effective remedy, and identifies significant regulatory gaps in the current framework. It concludes by proposing a rights-based, risk-sensitive and lifecycle-oriented framework for algorithmic accountability grounded in Indian constitutional principles rather than transplanted wholesale from foreign models.

items.title: Bridging the Human-AI preference gap: A persuasion-oriented tripartite framework
items.abstract: The remarkable performance of artificial intelligence (AI) systems on a wide variety of complex tasks has fueled its rapid adoption in recent years. Yet, many individuals still exhibit a human-AI preference gap , such that they prefer human-generated over AI-generated outputs and follow recommendations made by generative AI (GenAI) less than human advice. We conceptualize the rejection of a superior AI system in favor of an inferior human as a persuasion failure that necessitates psychological rather than technological resolution. Recent research has identified various interventions that compress the human-AI preference gap. We codify these interventions by introducing a persuasion-oriented tripartite framework that delineates three distinct paths by which the preference gap between humans and AI systems may be narrowed: (1) AI-centric interventions , which directly bolster perceptions and evaluations of AI systems; (2) human-centric interventions , which reduce the (often inflated) perceptions and evaluations of humans; and (3) hybrid interventions , which offer an integrated or reformulated alternative that combines human and AI elements. Ultimately, our tripartite framework illustrates how different persuasion tactics fundamentally reshape beliefs and attitudes about both AI and humans, thereby informing system design elements and communication strategies that can bridge the human-AI preference gap.

items.title: Characterising the ‘Genomics Friend’: Experiences of learning genomics in the workplace to inform implementation efforts
items.abstract: Abstract Large-scale genomic medicine implementation efforts are presenting relevant and authentic opportunities for the health workforce to learn genomics in the workplace, particularly from genomic expert colleagues or ‘champions’. This paper presents novel insights on genomic experts’ role and influence on learning genomics from the perspective of physicians not trained in genetics. As part of a study on workplace learning of genomics, longitudinal qualitative datasets were collected in 2021–2023 from ten non-genetics physicians working in hospitals in Victoria, Australia. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to characterise participants’ perceptions of, and workplace interactions with, genomic experts. Deductive content analysis was then applied to sort and synthesise participants’ relationships with genomics experts. Designated the ‘Genomics Friend’, these individuals are trained in genetics or recognised as same-specialty genomic champions and perceived as trusted and accessible sources of genomic expertise. Participants who had a Genomics Friend leveraged their established relationship on an ad hoc basis to address identified knowledge gaps. Sorting participants into the Genomics Friend Relationship Matrix demonstrated how having a Genomics Friend enhanced genomic workplace learning and practice for physicians across different career stages and specialties. These findings offer insights into how intra- and inter-disciplinary interactions and collegial relationships provide professional development opportunities through workplace learning. Moreover, we consider how genomic expert ‘friends’ could support implementation efforts by facilitating the health workforce to learn, adopt and practise genomics.

items.title: ChatGPT Use and Learning Motivation among Informatics Students: A Preliminary Correlational Study
items.abstract: Generative AI systems such as ChatGPT are increasingly used by university students for explanation, code inspection, idea generation, and immediate feedback. This preliminary cross-sectional study examines the association between ChatGPT use frequency and learning motivation among 17 Informatics Engineering students at Universitas Mulia, Balikpapan. Data were collected through an online questionnaire using a four-category measure of ChatGPT use frequency and four-point agreement responses for learning motivation. The original analysis reported a Pearson correlation of r = 0.685 with p = 0.002. Using the reported coefficient and sample size, the corresponding test statistic is t(15) = 3.642 and the Fisher-transformed 95% confidence interval is approximately 0.305-0.877, indicating a positive but imprecisely estimated association. The finding is consistent with literature suggesting that responsive AI tools may support engagement and perceived competence, but the correlational design does not establish that ChatGPT use increases motivation. Reverse causality, self-selection, prior achievement, digital confidence, purpose of use, and measurement limitations remain plausible explanations. The study contributes context-specific evidence from informatics students and identifies requirements for stronger follow-up research, including a larger sample, validated motivation measures, clearer characterization of AI use, rank-based sensitivity analysis, and longitudinal or quasi-experimental data.

items.title: Children, Robots, and Reproducibility: A review of recent reproducibility challenges in child-robot interaction
items.abstract: Given the rapid advancements and shifting requirements in the field of Child-Robot Interaction (CRI), it is crucial to understand how the field is evolving and if and how researchers are adhering to current best practices. We present a review of five years (2020-2024) of CRI research, under the lens of reproducibility. We analysed a total of 195 papers for transparency in reporting. We found deficiencies in reporting demographics (e.g., age of participants), study design and implementation (e.g. length of interactions), and open science practices (e.g., maintaining an active study repository). From our analysis, we identify a set of key challenges faced by CRI researchers and provide a checklist to systematically report CRI studies to help and guide research to improve reproducibility in CRI.

items.title: Comparing artificial intelligence versus human screening in systematic reviews
items.abstract: Systematic reviews are essential for informing health policy and practice. Artificial intelligence (AI) automates the article screening process and produces time savings, although the performance of AI screening compared to traditional human screening remains uncertain. We undertook this study to compare the performance of two agentic AI tools, namely Loon Lens TM and Catchii, to one another and to humans at the title and abstract screening level. We also compared Loon Lens to humans at the full-text screening level. We developed a de novo research question on the association between any of three ambient air pollutants – carbon monoxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide – and the onset or worsening of Parkinson’s disease. A health sciences librarian developed the literature search strategy and we proceeded with human and AI screening. Screening results were compared using sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, concordance, kappa, and F1 score. We contrasted these statistics to those obtained by naïve guessing and regressed concordance (agree or disagree with the human reference standard) onto confidence scores provided by Loon Lens, which assigned a confidence level (‘Very High’, ‘High’, Medium’, or ‘Low’) to each of its screening decisions. Human screening was the reference standard against both AI tools; Catchii was the reference standard against Loon Lens. At title and abstract screening, Loon Lens outperformed Catchii when humans were the reference standard (Loon Lens versus human: sensitivity = 0.66, kappa = 0.74, F1 = 0.76; Catchii versus human: sensitivity = 0.49, kappa = 0.46, F1 = 0.50). At full-text screening, most disagreements centered around articles Loon Lens included and humans excluded. At both screening levels, higher confidence scores were associated with lower odds of disagreement between Loon Lens and human screeners. Given the panoply of available AI screening tools and their differential performance, plus the rapidly evolving nature of AI technology, researchers should pilot test their chosen tool at the start of each review. Sensitivity, kappa, and F1 are the optimal performance statistics to employ, especially at title and abstract screening, where the imbalance between proportions of included and excluded citations can inflate concordance and negative predictive value.

items.title: Contract-Preserving Lower-to-Upper Recalibration in Hierarchical Agent Systems: An Integrated Framework
items.abstract: Soft and Hard De-Attraction (SHDA) specifies when verified lower-level recovery can support an upper-level revision without changing the external success contract. This condition is the framework's central axis, contract-preserving correctability: the joint condition, over separately judged coordinates, under which verified lower-level evidence may be admitted as the next correction and to which the system must return after each correction, containment, or revision. Because the components share budgets, strengthening one can break another; SHDA therefore organizes them as one closed loop along the axis, in which balance is an allocation of the shared budgets, not compensation. When a certified obligation fails, premise-level fault localization (T10) localizes the violation, within the recorded scope, to a false registered premise and its owner, a named record gap, or an unsound rule or checker; earliest failure sets diagnostic priority rather than establishing a causal mechanism. Under explicit assumptions, T1-T9 connect endogenous-error tracking, precision gates and probes, finite-phase progress, revision-aware certificate validity, transport between theorem epochs, repair costs, and same-episode outcomes. The scalar bounds and concentration tools are established ingredients; the proposed contribution is the integration layer: the objects, laws, and operations that exist only where the components meet. Three validation reports supply synthetic-loop tests (X3), planted-cause identification and fresh-audit repair comparisons (X2), and finite reachability checks (X1); their evidence is not interchangeable. In X2, certified full refresh matched budget-feasible diagnosis-guided repair in joint completion at nearly equal or lower cost, but a complete repair library and risk components with no failures observed in the retained runs left the repair value of diagnosis and risk untested; X1 separates post-fence compliance from safety under physical invalidation. The evidence supports scoped constructions and implementation obligations, not algorithmic superiority, deployed-agent safety, or unconditional convergence. Note on Version 2.0. This version replaces Version 1.0 (September 2026; about 9,200 words) and is a substantial revision (about 39,500 words). It organizes the framework around the contract-preserving correctability axis, adds premise-level fault localization (T10), states the conditional results as T1-T9, and adds three validation reports: finite reachability checks (X1), planted-cause identification and fresh-audit repair comparisons (X2) and synthetic-loop tests (X3). The Technical Supplement is revised as well (about 12,500 to 54,900 words). Files: the manuscript and the Technical Supplement as PDFs, and one supplement archive (132 files) with reproduction code, compact results and the validation reports. The Version 1.0 files remain available in the previous version of this record. Scope and status. This is the flagship of the Integrated Framework series on contract-preserving lower-to-upper recalibration (SHDA). The upload also contains the revised Technical Supplement, which states and proves T1-T9 and specifies the typed state, lineage, operations, attribution, disclosure and re-entry rules, the execution pipeline and the records. Companion A (residual genesis and dynamic feedback route attribution), Companion B (intervention-disclosure visibility and time-bounded selective nondisclosure), Companion C (family-scoped capability control, typed lineage and atomic re-entry) and the technical working paper SHDA Algorithms for Scoped Evidence Reuse and Recalibration are archived separately. The evidence consists of synthetic and finite-model checks; it does not establish deployed-agent safety or algorithmic superiority. AI use disclosure. Generative AI (GPT-6.0, OpenAI; Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) was used substantively in preparing this work, including source comparison, drafting and editing, and, where applicable, mathematical and counterexample checks and the writing and running of supplementary code. The research questions, framework and final claims were directed and reviewed by the author, who takes full responsibility for the content, including the accuracy of all references and reported numbers. items.title: Criteria for Assessing the Impact of Generative AI on Students' Dissertation Defences
items.abstract: This chapter explores the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) on students’ oral discourse during the defence of Final Degree Projects (Trabajo Fin de Título or TFT, in Spanish). It addresses a significant gap in research by focusing on GAI’s influence on spoken language, particularly in academic contexts like dissertation defences. The chapter also aims to establish criteria for evaluating oral defences in Spanish universities, with a special focus on GAI’s role in their preparation. Based on a review of literature from Scopus and Dialnet, and a comparison of evaluation criteria across fifteen Spanish universities, the chapter proposes key indicatorsfor assessing these defences. It identifies six core competences for evaluation: communication skills, language use, structure and coherence, time management, use of visual aids, and handling questions. Also, it suggests specific GAI-related signs (e.g. impersonal language, repetitive sentences, or unclear use of sources) to detect AI-generated content that could affect the assessment of TFT. The chapter emphasises the importance of ethical GAI use in oral presentations and concludes with proposals for the responsible integration of this technology into education to help students and educators reach their full potential.
